sentences.text: The largest known species, G. giganteus, could reach a maximum height of nearly 2 meters and weighed between 175 and 225 kilograms.
Its skull was huge relative to its body and built of powerful bone.
The beak of G. giganteus was extremely tall and compressed from side to side.
A single isolated feather found in the Green River Formation resembles the broad, vaned body feathers of flighted birds, indicating the animal once had wings.
Huge eggshell fragments were found in Late Paleocene deposits in Spain and early Eocene deposits in France, proving these birds laid massive eggs.
Tracks dated to about 53.7 million years old suggest they were made by Gastornis, with the largest known footprint impression measuring 40 cm in length.
The genus Gastornis was first described in 1855 by Hébert based on a fragmentary skeleton.
In 2020, a distinct species named G. laurenti was described based on specimens found near Saint-Papoul, southwestern France, making it the most recently described species of Gastornis.
Gastornis giganteus, formerly known as Diatryma gigantea, dates from the middle Eocene of western North America.

A long-standing debate involving Gastornis is the interpretation of its diet. It has frequently been represented as a predator of contemporary small mammals, the most famous of which is the primitive horse Eohippus. However, evidence including the lack of sharp claws and beak structure studies has led scientists to reinterpret Gastornis as herbivores that likely ate hard plant material and seeds. Studies of calcium isotopes in Gastornis specimens conducted by Thomas Tutken and colleagues did not show the presence of meat in their diet. The absence of raptor-like claws supports the hypothesis that Gastornis was a herbivore rather than a predator or scavenger. It may also have used its strong beak to eat large or very hard vegetation.
Gastornis is generally classified as related to the Galloanserae, which includes modern waterfowl and gamebirds.
Gastornis lived from the Paleocene to the middle Eocene epochs.
The earliest Gastornis fossils come from Europe, suggesting the genus likely originated there.

It is debated whether Diatryma is a junior synonym of Gastornis or a distinct valid genus. Scientists debate the synonymy of Gastornis and Diatryma because detailed comparisons of type specimens have not yet been completed.
Louchart et al. (2021) argued that there is no unambiguous evidence to support the synonymy of Omorhamphus storchii with Gastornis giganteus due to a lack of definitive juvenile specimens.
The reason for the extinction of Gastornis is currently unclear.
